description: Neolithic thresholds (spec peopling.md, section 3.6): where and when a local population of foragers is about to start farming or herding on its own. The tree's camps there settle; the farming plan continues from them.

thresholds.source: Zeder 2011, The origins of agriculture in the Near East, Current Anthropology 52 S4
Lombardo et al. 2020, Early Holocene crop cultivation and landscape modification in Amazonia, Nature 581 (crops from about 8300 BCE); farming villages and fields about 3500 BCE, approximate

Piperno & Flannery 2001, The earliest archaeological maize (Zea mays L.) from highland Mexico, PNAS 98 (maize at Guilá Naquitz about 4300 BCE; squash, Smith 1997, Science 276, was used from about 8000 BCE)

Dillehay et al. 2007, Preceramic adoption of peanut, squash, and cotton in northern Peru, Science 316 (cultivated plants from about 8000 BCE); farming with fields and irrigation about 3500 BCE, approximate

Lu et al. 2009, Earliest domestication of common millet (Panicum miliaceum) in East Asia extended to 10,000 years ago, PNAS 106 (first millet use); the date is that of the farming villages of Cishan and Peiligang, Zhao 2011, Current Anthropology 52 S4
Denham et al. 2003, Origins of agriculture at Kuk Swamp in the highlands of New Guinea, Science 301 (mounded cultivation, phase 2, from 6950 to 6440 cal BP; plant use there from about 8000 BCE)

Fuller et al. 2009, The domestication process and domestication rate in rice, Science 323 (rice cultivation at Kuahuqiao about 5750 BCE; first use at Shangshan, Zuo et al. 2017, PNAS 114, was earlier)
Jarrige et al. 1995, Mehrgarh: Field Reports 1974-1985, from Neolithic Times to the Indus Civilization
